claims.text: Low-temperature formation of noble-metal HEA nanoparticles can occur when precursor mobility is inhibited.
Inhibition of precursor mobility makes HEA nanoparticle formation governed by stochastic incorporation principles.
Stochastic incorporation produces a random atomic distribution of all constituent metals.
Inhibited precursor mobility favors formation of single-phase HEA nanoparticles and prevents phase segregation.
The relevant precursor system contains both cationic and anionic noble-metal single-source precursors.
The precursors begin as a well-mixed solution or solid precipitate.
At low synthesis temperatures, the entropy contribution to alloy formation is minor.
Controlled cooling rates under the proposed low-temperature conditions suppress precursor diffusion.
Combining five noble metals favors single-phase nanoparticle formation relative to bimetallic mixtures.
Bimetallic systems are more prone to partial phase separation because they contain fewer competing species.
Partial phase separation in bimetallic nanoparticles produces a heterogeneous distribution of catalytic sites.
Uniform atomic mixing in five-element HEA nanoparticles produces a more even distribution of active sites.
A more even active-site distribution improves catalytic activity through synergy among active sites.
The studied five-metal Pt-Ir-Os-Rh-Ru precursor system has superior oxygen-reduction catalytic activity.
Five-element HEA nanoparticles will outperform bimetallic nanoparticles catalytically when both are synthesized under identical low-temperature conditions.
The proposed performance advantage may be observed in oxygen reduction or nitrobenzene hydrogenation.
The formation hypothesis should apply broadly to noble-metal nanoparticles made by low-temperature solution-based or low-energy reduction methods with limited precursor mobility.
The hypothesis may not apply under high-temperature or high-diffusivity conditions where entropy-driven stabilization dominates.
In situ X-ray powder diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy can track crystallization, phase formation, elemental reduction, and local chemical states in this system.
